takeaway: In this review, opioids were not more effective than placebo for breathlessness (SMD −0.14; 95% CI −0.47 to 0.18), and anxiolytics were not more effective than placebo either [1].
clinicalQuestion: Do opioids or anxiolytics improve breathlessness in advanced cancer?
background: Oncology guidelines have endorsed opioids and anxiolytics, often from older data and from studies that excluded cancer [1].
setting: Studies of adults with advanced cancer, searched through 31 May 2020.
population: 1424 patients in 19 studies (17 randomised trials and 2 retrospective studies). Lung cancer was the most common cancer reported [1].
intervention: Pharmacologic treatments, principally opioids and anxiolytics.
comparator: Placebo, or another dose or route of opioid.
primaryOutcome: Breathlessness, with anxiety, exercise capacity, and quality of life also examined.
mainFindings: Opioids were not associated with more effectiveness than placebo for breathlessness (SMD −0.14; 95% CI −0.47 to 0.18) or exercise capacity (SMD 0.06; 95% CI −0.43 to 0.55); strength of evidence moderate. Most opioid studies examined exertional breathlessness. Dose or route did not differ (SMD 0.15; 95% CI −0.22 to 0.52; low strength of evidence). Anxiolytics were not more effective than placebo for breathlessness or anxiety (mean difference −0.52; 95% CI −1.045 to 0.005; low strength of evidence). Dropout from adverse events in these short studies was 3.2% to 16%. The authors say drugs may be considered in selected patients, alongside harms and the evidence that nonpharmacologic interventions are associated with improved breathlessness [1].
clinicalMeaning: A routine opioid or benzodiazepine for cancer breathlessness is not supported by this evidence. Selection and harms still matter, and non-drug measures are the interventions this review points to [1].
limitations: Studies were short, often of exertional breathlessness, and many estimates have low strength of evidence. This is not a licence to withhold a carefully chosen opioid from a distressed dying patient; it is a statement of the trial evidence [1].
bottomLine: Do not teach that opioids outperform placebo for breathlessness in advanced cancer. This meta-analysis did not find that [1].
practiceImplication: Discuss a fan or other non-drug measure, and if a drug is used, do it for a selected patient with an explicit look at harm [1].
safetyOutcomes: Some harms versus usual care were seen; dropout attributed to adverse events was 3.2–16%.
trustRationale: Prespecified meta-analysis, limited by short trials and low strength of evidence for several comparisons.
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not quote a fan effect size from this pharmacologic paper; it is not reported here.
Do not convert the null finding into a prohibition in the last hours of life.
